newsitem.title: SWEDEN: FOCUS - Sweden counts cost of self-imposed isolation.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Sweden counts cost of self-imposed isolation.

text.p: The crown remained firm and interest rates held steady on Monday as Sweden counted the cost of its chosen isolation from the Exchange Rate Mechanism (ERM) grid, now linking 12 of the European Union's 15 countries.
Italy's re-admittance to the ERM left some Swedes dismayed about their growing isolation while others said nothing had changed and the real test still lay ahead.
The three ERM outsiders are now "Britain, which doesn't want to join, Greece, which can't, and Sweden which thinks it doesn't need to," the evening daily Expressen summarised.

Swedish financial markets were little moved by the lira factor, confounding some pessimists who had predicted the crown and bond prices would be immediately punished for Stockholm's stubborn refusal to follow neighbour Finland, and now Italy, into the ERM.
"I do not think there will be any major repercussions," said Professor Lars Calmfors of Stockholm University.
"The lira's re-entry was not unexpected. It has been on the cards for some time now. It will have more of an impact if Italy joins EMU at the outset, and this is an open question."

At the official level, central bank governor Urban Backstrom and Finance Minister Erik Asbrink said nothing had changed and repeated that Sweden would make up its mind in a year's time on whether or not to enter Europe's economic and monetary union (EMU).

A government commission led by Professor Calmfors into the consequences of Swedish participation in EMU concluded this month that the arguments against joining in 1999 were stronger than those in favour.
Newspapers wondered aloud on Monday whether Sweden, located on the geographical fringe of Europe, could afford to be politically sidelined as well.
"If Sweden does not want to be in the inner circle now, is it waiting to join or have we definitely decided not to join?" the daily Svenska Dagbladet pondered.
The price for prevarication and delay could be that Sweden's partners may be less understanding when it asked for special favours such as an exemption on alcohol policy, the paper warned.

Expressen also bemoaned that Sweden was looking more and more like an outsider at the EU table, and it predicted that Prime Minister Goran Persson would feel the chill at the EU summit in Dublin next month.
"We said it was a trade-off, with the economic arguments offset by perhaps some loss of political influence," Calmfors told Reuters.

Handelsbanken chief economist Carl B.Hamilton said: "Italy's entry leads again to unflattering comparisons between Italy, Finland and others on the one hand, and the 'reluctant Europeans' on the other, such as Britain and Sweden."
The strongly falling trend of long-term yields enjoyed by Finland, Italy and Spain showed clearly that attitudes towards ERM and EMU have an impact on interest rates, Hamilton noted.
Asbrink said in a statement on Sunday night: "It is still the government's perception that it is not a current issue for Sweden to link the crown to the ERM.

"Since November 1992 Sweden has a floating exchange rate. Price stability is the overriding aim for monetary and exchange rate policy. This approach has been successful and there is no reason to change it."
Sweden maintains that with the best inflation record in Europe, and rapidly improving public sector finances, it can afford to go it alone and still meet EMU convergence criteria.

Calmfors said Britain and/or Denmark joining would have a greater impact on Sweden but that German public opinion, deciding whether or not to abandon the cherished mark in favour of the euro, would ultimately determine the extent of EMU.
